t: How To Refocus Your Students Back On School
q: Over the past year, educational standards have fallen like a rodeo cowboy.
Here at SCM, however, we believe it’s best to get them right back up on the horse.
A push for excellence in anything , regardless of what it is, fires the motivational engines. It generates thoughts of the future, which is extraordinarily healthy to both body and mind.
Purpose is the driver for every worthy pursuit in our lives. Without it, there is nothing but empty entertainment and momentary pleasure.
Having purpose, even on a small scale, is highly motivational. Without the why it’s hard for students to see the point.
Together—excellence, purpose, urgency—will not only get your students back up on the horse, but galloping into their future.
x: Writing as students return from a year of pandemic disruption, Linsin argues against easing them back in gently and instead advocates pushing hard to refocus them right away.

He frames purpose as something that can operate at both the macro level of long-term goals and the micro level of a single day's lesson, arguing that without an explicit 'why,' students struggle to see the point of their work.
The piece closes by tying these three elements — excellence, purpose, urgency — together as the combination needed to fully re-engage a demoralized, pandemic-affected class.

t: Helping Teachers Do the Very Hard Thing
q: At Desmos, we’re convinced by a variety of research, personal experience, and trusted testimony that the most productive change a math teacher can make is to develop an asset orientation toward their students’ thinking.

It’s also digital. Students express a lot of that brilliance in a form that’s visible to teachers and the people who support teachers, including site-based coaches and coaches at Desmos. Teachers are able to enact some sophisticated routines through the platform like selecting student ideas, sequencing them, and presenting them.

Lots of curricula is one or the other. The IM curriculum is extremely rich but print-first. Lots of digital curricula only make room for student brilliance in the form of multiple choice responses and numbers—stuff that computers often grade as correct or incorrect.

We offer teachers a large kick-off session at the start of the school year to get us lined up on some of our hopes and dreams for the year and to get us excited for the work. This session is high intensity and one-time only, and we know the energy and learning dissipates quickly.

For example, teachers are always in their email. Let’s use that as a medium for professional learning. We know what lesson a teacher taught yesterday, so we send that teacher an email previewing the next lesson through the lens of one of the three themes, which we spiral throughout the year: inviting student brilliance, celebrating it, and developing it, with pedagogical techniques attached.

We offer those ideas to teachers not in a one-off session abstracted from their daily work, but rather as close to the teacher’s practice as we can get: “On this screen, here’s a great moment to tell students, ‘Look, you can’t break mathematics.’ ” These preview emails give teachers essential and generalizable teaching strategies and give us email open rates that email marketers can only dream about.

q: After all, the students you saw online aren’t the same ones you’re seeing in person. Oh, they have the same names. They look the same.
The upside down has turned right side up. That virtual reality environment you taught in, along with the two-dimensional relationship you had with your students, is gone.
You remember that for all practical purposes the day your students returned to the classroom was the first day of school. And it needed to be treated as such.
You pretend it is the first day of school. You say simply, “I’m not happy with how things are going. It’s my fault, not yours, and here is what we’re going to do about it.
Take control of your classroom with boldness and good cheer. Throw a happy shock to their system by setting a sky-high bar of excellence.

t: 9 Ways To Be A Smarter, Mentally Sharper Teacher
q: Mental acuity is an often-overlooked aspect of good teaching and absolutely essential for effective classroom management.
You need at least seven hours of sleep , and preferably more. Otherwise, you won’t have the willpower and clarity needed to consistently manage your class.
Focus is a constant awareness of your immediate objective and being fully present in the moment . So lock in.
Listening is a superpower that gives you so much more insight and empathy than the average teacher. It allows you to predict, understand, and always know just what to say.
You’re at your mental peak first thing in the morning and will make better and more efficient decisions than in the afternoon.
You don’t have to embrace every suggestion above. Just a handful, or even two or three, can make a big difference. The key is to start slow.

t: How To Effectively Send A Student To Time-Out https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2021/04/09/how-to-effectively-send-a-student-to-time-out/
q: You can call it time-out, time away, observation mode or anything you like, but the way you send a student there matters.
Clarity is key to getting students to go to time-out willingly and benefiting from it. It’s key to them reflecting on their misbehavior and resolving not to make the same mistake again.
You’re not a judge. You’re just a referee doing their job , calling em’ like you see em.’ Your neutrality helps shift the responsibility for misbehavior entirely to the student.
To that end, never walk students to time-out. Never show displeasure or outward disappointment. Just stick with the script above.
Furthermore, you mustn’t tell them how they should’ve behaved or what they should think or feel about their mistake. No lecturing, counseling, or pulling aside for a talking-to.
Quite simply, it has the power to not only remove your stress related to enforcing consequences, but to very effectively curb misbehavior.
x: Students should never be walked to time-out or shown visible displeasure, both of which reinsert the teacher into the consequence.

A neutral, 'referee' tone during enforcement shifts full responsibility for the misbehavior onto the student rather than the teacher.

t: Why So Many Teachers Struggle With Classroom Management https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2021/04/03/teachers-struggle-with-classroom-management/
q: Allow me to let you in on a secret: There is a shocking difference between classrooms run by teachers with excellent classroom management and everyone else.
The result is that teachers enter the profession unprepared. They lose confidence and quit or spend the rest of their career pretending to be a good teacher.
The deeper reason that there is such a profound difference between good teachers and the rest, however, is what I call the great disconnect.
If you don’t know what’s possible, if you’ve never seen whole-class transformation, then it’s hard to believe it exists.
It isn’t quantum physics. There are skills you can learn that will allow you to walk into any classroom in the world and transform those students into your dream class .
If you don’t believe me, give us a chance to prove it to you. Put SCM to the test for one month.
x: The scale of difference between classrooms run by excellent versus average classroom managers is described as far larger than most teachers assume.
Linsin argues that the gap between excellent and average classrooms is far larger than most teachers realize, and traces it to what he calls 'the great disconnect'.
'The great disconnect' — never having witnessed real whole-class transformation — is identified as the deepest reason teachers doubt it's possible.
